text: Chapter 7 covered working with scientists and feedback inside the research phase. This chapter crosses a different boundary — the moment a result stops being a checkpoint that beat the baseline and starts being something another team has to run and serve without you in the room. That transition fails more often from a bad handoff than from a bad model.

A raw checkpoint plus a Slack message is not a handoff — it's how a production team ends up reverse-engineering your preprocessing three months later, usually during an incident. A real handoff packages the model as a self-contained inference artifact, pins the exact preprocessing code, ships an eval score and a known-good input/output pair for parity checks, and includes a model card plus an owner's name for when the model starts behaving strangely.

TorchScript captures a model as a graph loadable without your original Python class. Tracing is the simplest path, recording one execution of the forward pass — it's the right default unless the model has real data-dependent control flow, in which case torch.jit.script compiles the actual logic instead of baking in a single branch.

ONNX targets interoperability — the same export can be loaded by Triton, ONNX Runtime, or non-PyTorch stacks, which matters when the production team's serving infrastructure isn't PyTorch-specific. The detail that bites people in practice is dynamic_axes: without it, the exported graph hardcodes the batch size from whatever example input you traced with.

With the model packaged and its assumptions written down, the next question is how it actually gets served. Lesson 39 covers productionization trade-offs — latency, throughput, and cost pull in different directions, and the right serving choice depends on which one you're optimizing for.
